title: Parallel structure and concise writing
blurb: Make lists, pairs, comparisons and correlative pairs match in form, and cut redundant, wordy phrases without losing meaning.
question: A résumé bullet reads, “Responsibilities included greeting patients, to answer phones, and I scheduled appointments in order to reduce wait times.” Which parts break the pattern, and what is the tightest correct version?

teach.body: Formally, parallel structure means that items joined in a series, a pair or a comparison share the same grammatical form: all nouns, all -ing words, all to-verbs, all clauses. Plain English: once you start a pattern, keep it. “Reading, hiking, and swimming” is parallel; “reading, hiking, and to swim” breaks the pattern. Concise writing is the partner skill: say it once, in the fewest clear words.

teach.caption: Joining words (and, or, but, than, as) are signals: whatever sits on one side must match what sits on the other.

steps.label: Find the joiner
steps.sub: and, or, but, than, both/and, not only/but also

head: Pattern
Parallel example
rows: greeting visitors, answering phones, and filing charts
to listen, to explain, and to reassure
greeted visitors, answered phones, and filed charts
that she was ready and that she had studied

teach.h: Correlative pairs: the same thing after each half
teach.body: Both ... and, either ... or, neither ... nor, and not only ... but also come in pairs, and the words right after each half must match. “We will meet either at noon or at three” puts a phrase after each half. “We will either meet at noon or at three” puts a verb after either but a phrase after or. Also keep the full pair: not only ... but also, not “not only ... and also.”

Concise writing removes redundancy (saying the same idea twice, as in “end result” or “repeat again”) and wordiness (long phrases that a single word can replace, as in “due to the fact that”). Concise does not mean shortest at any cost: the revision must keep the full meaning and stay grammatical. A short option that creates a comma splice or drops a needed idea is wrong.

Nursing applicant Brianna Lopez wrote: “Responsibilities included greeting patients, to answer phones, and I scheduled appointments in order to reduce wait times.” The three items are an -ing phrase, a to-verb and a full clause, so the pattern breaks. “Responsibilities included” and “in order to” add words without meaning. Revised: “Greeted patients, answered phones, and scheduled appointments to reduce wait times.” Three past-tense verbs, no padding.

teach.text: Two traps share this objective. First, a non-parallel item hidden at the END of a list sounds natural because you have stopped listening; check the last item hardest. Second, in “most concise” items, the shortest option often introduces a new error (a comma splice or a lost idea), so check that the concise answer is still correct.

items: Items in a series, pair or comparison share one grammatical form.
Check the item after the last and or or; that is where the break usually hides.
Correlative pairs (both/and, either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also) take matching elements after each half.
Cut redundancy (end result, past history, repeat again) and wordiness (due to the fact that, in order to).
The most concise answer must still be grammatical and keep the full meaning.
Prefer who for people; use that or which for things.

summary: You can now make series, pairs, comparisons and correlative pairs parallel, and spot the break that usually hides in the last item. You can also cut redundant and wordy phrases while keeping a sentence complete and correct.

options: The aide's tasks are bathing patients, changing linens, and to restock supplies.
The aide's tasks are bathing patients, changing linens, and restocking supplies.
The aide's tasks are to bathe patients, changing linens, and restocking supplies.
The aide's tasks are bathing patients, to change linens, and restocking supplies.
A.why: All three items are -ing phrases: bathing, changing, restocking.

whyNot.0: The last item switches to a to-verb (to restock).
whyNot.2: The first item is a to-verb (to bathe) while the others use -ing.
whyNot.3: The middle item is a to-verb (to change) while the others use -ing.

A.q: Which sentence uses the correlative pair correctly?
options: The program is not only affordable but also flexible.
The program not only is affordable but also flexible.
The program is not only affordable but also it is flexible.
The program is both affordable and it is flexible.
A.why: An adjective follows each half of the pair: not only affordable, but also flexible.

whyNot.1: A verb (is affordable) follows not only, but an adjective (flexible) follows but also.
whyNot.2: An adjective follows not only, but a clause (it is flexible) follows but also.
whyNot.3: An adjective follows both, but a clause (it is flexible) follows and.

A.q: Which revision of “Due to the fact that the lab was closed, the results were delayed” is most concise and still correct?
options: Owing to the fact that the lab was closed, results were delayed.
Because of the fact that the lab was closed, results were delayed.
Because the lab was closed, the results were delayed.
The lab was closed, the results were delayed.
A.why: Because replaces the five-word phrase “due to the fact that” with no change in meaning.

whyNot.0: “Owing to the fact that” is just as wordy as the original.
whyNot.1: “Because of the fact that” keeps the padding “of the fact that.”
whyNot.3: Shorter, but it joins two independent clauses with only a comma: a comma splice.

B.q: Which comparison is written in parallel form?
options: Walking to class is healthier than to drive.
To walk to class is healthier than driving.
Walking to class is healthier than if you drive.
Walking to class is healthier than driving.
B.why: Both sides of than use an -ing form: walking ... driving.

whyNot.0: Walking (-ing) is compared with to drive (to-verb).
whyNot.1: To walk (to-verb) is compared with driving (-ing).
whyNot.2: Walking (-ing) is compared with a clause (if you drive).

B.q: Which sentence contains NO redundant wording?
options: The clinic is close to the bus stop on Main Street.
The end result of the study surprised the researchers.
The patient's past history includes asthma and eczema.
Please repeat the instructions again for the new aide.
B.why: Every word adds meaning; there is no repeated idea.

whyNot.1: A result is already the end: “end result” is redundant.
whyNot.2: History is already in the past: “past history” is redundant.
whyNot.3: Repeat already means do again: “repeat ... again” is redundant.

B.q: Which sentence places either ... or correctly?
options: She will either take the TEAS in May or in June.
She will take the TEAS either in May or in June.
She either will take the TEAS in May or June.
Either she will take the TEAS in May or in June.
B.why: A prepositional phrase follows each half: either in May, or in June.

whyNot.0: Either is followed by a verb (take) but or by a phrase (in June).
whyNot.2: Either is followed by a verb (will take) but or by a noun (June).
whyNot.3: Either is followed by a clause (she will take) but or by a phrase (in June).

C.q: An applicant wrote, “In my role as a volunteer, I greeted visitors, was answering phones, and helped in the process of scheduling appointments.” Which revision is both parallel and concise?
options: As a volunteer, I greeted visitors, answered phones, and was scheduling appointments.
In my role as a volunteer, I greeted visitors, answered phones, and scheduled appointments.
As a volunteer, I greeted visitors, answered phones, and scheduled appointments.
As a volunteer, I greeted visitors, answering phones, and scheduled appointments.
C.why: Three simple past verbs (greeted, answered, scheduled), and “As a volunteer” replaces the wordy “In my role as a volunteer.”

whyNot.0: Was scheduling breaks the pattern of simple past verbs.
whyNot.1: Parallel, but “In my role as” is wordier than “As,” so it is not the most concise.
whyNot.3: Answering (-ing) breaks the pattern of past-tense verbs.

options: The applicant was nervous, tired, and hungry.
She prefers studying at night to studying at dawn.
We can meet in the library or at the cafe.
He likes to swim, to run, and biking on weekends.
C.why: Two to-verbs (to swim, to run) are followed by an -ing word (biking), which breaks the pattern.

whyNot.1: Parallel: studying ... studying on both sides of the comparison.
whyNot.2: Parallel: two prepositional phrases joined by or.

C.q: In “At this point in time, the clinic is not accepting new patients,” which replacement for “At this point in time” is most concise without changing the meaning?
options: Currently
At this moment in time
As of this current point
At the present time
C.why: Currently says “now” in one word with the same meaning.

whyNot.1: Still wordy: it simply swaps point for moment.
whyNot.2: Wordy and redundant: current and “this point” say the same thing.
whyNot.3: Correct in meaning but four words where one will do.

reteach.title: A matching uniform for every item
reteach.question: Picture a team photo where everyone wears the same uniform except one player in pajamas. Why does that one player stand out, and how does that help you find parallelism errors?

blocks.body: In a list, every item is a team member. If two wear -ing uniforms (greeting, answering) and the third wears a to-verb uniform (to schedule), the third looks wrong. Change the odd one, not the whole team. Concise writing is the same photo with no one standing in it twice: “end result” is the result posing beside itself.

blocks.h: Find the player out of uniform

blocks.text: The out-of-uniform item is usually last in line. Read the final item of every list against the first.

explain.body: Every item in a list of two or more takes the same form as the first: nouns with nouns, -ing with -ing, to-verbs with to-verbs.

test.q: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? “The nursing program values honesty, teamwork, and ___.”
options: being compassionate
compassion
to be compassionate
that you are compassionate
test.why: Honesty and teamwork are nouns, so the third item must be a noun: compassion.

whyNot.0: Being compassionate is an -ing phrase, not a noun like the others.
whyNot.2: To be compassionate is a to-verb phrase, not a noun.
whyNot.3: A clause does not match two single nouns.

explain.body: Whatever sits on one side of than, as, or, or and must match what sits on the other side.

test.q: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? “Reviewing notes daily is more effective than ___ the night before.”
options: to cram
if you cram
cramming
you cram
test.why: Reviewing is an -ing form, so the other side of than needs cramming.

whyNot.0: To cram is a to-verb and does not match reviewing.
whyNot.1: A clause (if you cram) does not match the -ing subject.
whyNot.3: A clause (you cram) does not match the -ing subject.

explain.body: Both/and, either/or, neither/nor and not only/but also must be complete pairs, and each half must be followed by the same kind of element.

head: Pair
Parallel example
rows: not only for nurses but also for aides
neither on Monday nor on Tuesday

test.q: Which choice correctly completes the sentence? “The workshop is designed not only for new nurses ___.”
options: but experienced aides also
and also for experienced aides
but also experienced aides
but also for experienced aides
test.why: Not only is followed by “for new nurses,” so but also needs the same structure: “for experienced aides.”

whyNot.0: Drops for and splits but also, so the halves do not match.
whyNot.1: Not only must pair with but also, not and also.
whyNot.2: Missing for, so a phrase is matched with a bare noun.

explain.body: Delete words that repeat an idea already stated and replace long phrases with one precise word, keeping the meaning and the grammar intact.

options: new patient
free gift
past week
first visit
test.why: A gift is already free, so “free gift” says the same thing twice.

whyNot.0: New adds meaning: a patient can be new or returning.
whyNot.2: Past adds meaning: it identifies which week.
whyNot.3: First adds meaning: it identifies which visit.
